items.prompt: Which gas is the largest contributor to human-caused warming through its rising concentration in the atmosphere?

options.label: Water vapour from oceans
Carbon dioxide
Methane from livestock
Nitrous oxide from soils

rubric: CO2 from fossil fuels and land use is the largest driver of human-caused warming.
Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of air but do not absorb infrared radiation significantly.

items.prompt: What term describes the fraction of incoming sunlight that a surface reflects back to space?

options.label: Insolation
Albedo
Salinity
Emissivity

rubric: Albedo is the reflectivity of a surface.
Emissivity concerns emitted radiation; insolation is incoming solar energy.

items.prompt: Which of these is a greenhouse gas released by livestock digestion and rice paddies?

options.label: Neon
Nitrogen
Methane
Oxygen

rubric: Methane (CH4) is produced by ruminants and flooded rice fields.
Helium and neon are noble gases and not greenhouse gases.

items.prompt: Which natural archive provides air bubbles that record atmospheric composition going back hundreds of thousands of years?

options.label: Tree rings
Ice cores
Coral skeletons
Lake sediments

rubric: Ice cores trap ancient air bubbles directly.
Tree rings, corals and sediments record climate indirectly and do not hold ancient air.

items.prompt: What is the name of the process by which plants take in CO2 from the air and store carbon in their tissues?

options.label: Respiration
Photosynthesis
Combustion
Evaporation

rubric: Photosynthesis removes CO2 and builds organic carbon.
Respiration and combustion release CO2; evaporation concerns water.

items.prompt: Which of the following are major reservoirs (stores) in the global carbon cycle? Select all that apply.

options.label: The oceans
Fossil fuel deposits
Atmospheric nitrogen gas (N2)
Soils and vegetation

rubric: Oceans, fossil fuels, and soils/vegetation all store large amounts of carbon.
The Moon is not part of Earth's carbon cycle.

items.prompt: A student reads a climate report that gives global temperatures as 'anomalies'. What does a temperature anomaly of +1.0 °C mean?

options.label: The measurement could be off by 1.0 °C either way
The temperature is 1.0 °C above the freezing point
The temperature is 1.0 °C above a reference average
The temperature is exactly 1.0 °C everywhere on Earth

rubric: An anomaly is a departure from a reference average.
Other options confuse anomaly with absolute value or error.

items.prompt: Why does adding CO2 to the atmosphere warm the lower atmosphere?

options.label: It absorbs outgoing infrared radiation and re-emits some back toward the surface
It absorbs incoming visible sunlight high in the atmosphere and passes that heat down to the ground
It forms a solid layer that stops infrared radiation from leaving Earth at all
It reflects incoming sunlight back to space more strongly, leaving more heat in the air

rubric: Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit infrared, slowing heat loss.
Reflecting sunlight would cool; heat is slowed, not blocked entirely.

items.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes weather from climate?

options.label: Weather is global while climate is local
Climate is the long-term average of weather over decades
Climate refers only to temperature, weather only to rain
Weather lasts months while climate lasts days

rubric: Climate is statistics of weather over about 30 years or more.
Other options reverse time scales or limit variables.

items.prompt: Why does melting sea ice amplify warming?

options.label: Dark open water absorbs more sunlight than bright ice does
Melting ice releases stored heat into the air above it as it thaws
Melting ice adds dissolved CO2 to the ocean, which then warms it
Meltwater evaporates and the vapor traps heat that ice would reflect

rubric: Lower albedo of open water is the ice-albedo feedback.
Other options invent mechanisms not driving this feedback.

items.prompt: Why is the natural greenhouse effect important for life on Earth?

options.label: It produces the oxygen that animals need to breathe
It shields the surface from all of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light
It stops the Sun from heating the oceans too much
It keeps the average surface temperature well above freezing

rubric: Without it the average surface would be about -18 °C.
The ozone layer, not the greenhouse effect, handles UV.

items.prompt: What happens to much of the CO2 that humans emit when burning fossil fuels?

options.label: Plants and the stratosphere break it down into oxygen within a few years
Nearly all of it dissolves in the oceans, so the air keeps little
Nearly all of it stays in the air, since land and oceans cannot take it up
Part stays in the air while the rest is absorbed by oceans and land

rubric: Roughly half is taken up by oceans and land sinks; the rest accumulates.
Other options overstate or invent fates.

items.prompt: Which of these are examples of evidence that Earth has warmed in recent decades? Select all that apply.

options.label: Increasing ocean heat content
Growing number of cold winter days in the Arctic
Retreating mountain glaciers
Increasing extent of summer Arctic sea ice

items.prompt: A friend says, 'It snowed heavily this week, so global warming must be false.' You explain the difference between a single weather event and a long-term trend. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.label: Heavy snow shows the local climate is cooling, and a warming planet could not produce it
Climate scientists leave unusually cold days out of their datasets so the warming trend looks steady
One snowy week is local, short-term weather; climate trends come from many years of global data
Global warming means every place gets warmer every single day, so any cold spell disproves the trend

rubric: Weather variability does not contradict a long-term global trend.
Other options misstate what warming implies.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains how greenhouse gases warm Earth's surface?

options.label: They trap warm surface air so it cannot rise into the upper atmosphere and escape
They release heat when they react chemically with ozone high in the atmosphere
They absorb infrared from the surface and re-emit some of it back downward
They reflect incoming visible sunlight back down toward the surface of the Earth

rubric: Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit part of it toward the surface, slowing heat loss to space.
Distractors confuse the effect with reflection of sunlight, a physical 'lid' on convection, or chemical heat release.

items.prompt: Which example is a positive (amplifying) climate feedback?

options.label: Extra evaporation forms clouds that cool the surface
Faster plant growth removes extra CO2 from the air
Hotter surfaces emit more infrared, limiting further warming
Warmer oceans absorb less CO2, so more stays airborne

rubric: Reduced ocean CO2 uptake in warmer water leaves more CO2 in the air and amplifies warming.
Distractors describe negative feedbacks, which dampen the initial warming.

items.prompt: Why are air bubbles trapped in polar ice cores useful for studying past climate?

options.label: They hold samples of ancient air showing past greenhouse gas levels
They reveal past sea level by the depth at which the bubbles sit in the ice
They record past ocean currents by the size and shape of each bubble
They show past sunspot counts through the chemical makeup of their gases

rubric: Bubbles are sealed samples of ancient atmosphere, so CO2 and methane can be measured directly.
Distractors assign unrelated proxy roles to the bubbles.

items.prompt: A region has an unusually cold week in winter. What does this event most reasonably show about climate?

options.label: It shows greenhouse gases have stopped trapping heat in that region
It shows that the long-term global warming trend has paused for now
It is normal weather variability, not a climate trend
It shows the climate of that region has begun shifting toward cooling

rubric: Climate is the average over decades, so one cold week is weather variability.
Distractors treat a short local event as a trend or as a change in physics.

items.prompt: Why does burning fossil fuels raise atmospheric CO2 more than plant respiration does over time?

options.label: Respiration releases CO2 so slowly that it only adds up over many centuries
Plants take up all the CO2 that respiration releases within each day
It moves carbon stored for millions of years into the fast surface cycle
Fossil fuels release far more CO2 per kilogram of carbon than respiring plants do

rubric: Fossil burning adds new carbon from a long-term geological reservoir; respiration recycles carbon already in the surface system.
Distractors misstate rates or claim plants fully offset respiration daily.

items.prompt: Which observations support the conclusion that recent CO2 rise is mainly from fossil fuel burning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Volcanoes emit more CO2 each year than humans do
Measured solar output has risen steadily since 1980
Atmospheric carbon has a lower 13C share, matching fossil-derived carbon
Atmospheric CO2 rose in step with cumulative human emissions
The ocean surface has become more basic over the same period

rubric: Isotope shifts and the match with emission totals both point to fossil sources.
Distractors cite a false solar trend, a false volcano claim, and the reverse of ocean acidification.

items.prompt: A news report says the average pH of the ocean surface has fallen over the past century as CO2 has risen. A student asks why more atmospheric CO2 would make seawater more acidic. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions
Extra CO2 traps heat that warms the surface water, and the warmer water always has a lower pH
CO2 reacts with the chloride in seawater salt to form hydrochloric acid directly
CO2 displaces dissolved oxygen from the water, and the oxygen loss makes the water acidic

rubric: CO2 + H2O forms carbonic acid, which dissociates and adds hydrogen ions, lowering pH.
Distractors invent hydrochloric acid, overstate temperature effects, or blame oxygen loss.

items.prompt: Solar constant is 1361 W/m^2 and Earth's albedo is 0.30. Using S/4 x (1 - albedo), what is the average absorbed solar energy per square metre of Earth's surface?
rubric: 1361/4 = 340; times 0.70 gives about 238 W/m^2.
Distractors skip the division by 4, skip the albedo, or use 0.30 instead of 0.70.

items.prompt: Humans emit 10 GtC per year, and 45% stays in the air. Given that 1 ppm of CO2 is about 2.1 GtC, about how much does CO2 rise in a year?

options.label: 0.9 ppm
2.1 ppm
10 ppm
4.8 ppm

rubric: 10 x 0.45 = 4.5 GtC airborne; divided by 2.1 gives about 2.1 ppm.
Distractors forget the airborne fraction, or multiply instead of dividing.

items.prompt: Doubling CO2 gives a radiative forcing of 3.7 W/m^2. If the climate responds with 0.8 K of warming per W/m^2 at equilibrium, what is the expected warming?

options.label: About 1.2 K
About 3.0 K
About 0.8 K
About 4.6 K

rubric: 3.7 x 0.8 is about 3.0 K.
Distractors divide instead of multiply, or report the sensitivity parameter itself.

items.prompt: Global mean sea level is rising at a steady 3.5 mm per year. How much will it rise in 30 years if the rate stays constant?

options.label: About 1.05 cm
About 105 cm
About 10.5 cm
About 35 cm

rubric: 3.5 mm x 30 = 105 mm, which is 10.5 cm.
Distractors slip by a factor of 10 in unit conversion or use the wrong multiplier.

items.prompt: A large volcanic eruption injects a lot of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere. What is the most likely effect on global average temperature over the next one to two years?

options.label: A permanent cooling that lasts for several centuries
A slight cooling, as sulfate aerosols reflect sunlight
A strong warming, as the ash traps outgoing infrared
No change, as volcanic gases stay near the ground

rubric: Stratospheric sulfate aerosols reflect sunlight and cool the surface for a year or two until they fall out.
Distractors reverse the sign, claim no effect, or treat the cooling as permanent.

items.prompt: Which actions would lower net atmospheric CO2 over the coming decades? Select all that apply.

options.label: Draining peatlands to convert them to cropland
Regrowing forest on land that was cleared for farming
Burning stored wood waste in open piles each year
Capturing CO2 at a power plant and storing it underground

rubric: Regrowth and geological storage both remove or keep CO2 out of the air.
Draining peat and open burning release stored carbon.

items.prompt: An analyst reads that preindustrial CO2 was about 280 ppm and that today it is about 420 ppm. A colleague asks what percentage increase this is relative to the preindustrial level. Which value should the analyst report?
rubric: The rise is 140 ppm, and 140/280 = 0.50, so 50%.
Distractors divide by the present value, give the ratio minus nothing, or misuse the base.

items.prompt: Global mean albedo falls from 0.30 to 0.25 as sea ice melts. With a solar constant of 1361 W/m^2, what is the change in global-mean absorbed solar flux, using S(1 - albedo)/4?
rubric: Change = 1361 x 0.05 / 4, about 17 W/m^2.
Distractor 68 omits the division by 4 for sphere geometry.

items.prompt: Use ΔF = 5.35 ln(C/C0) W/m^2 and a climate sensitivity parameter of 0.8 K per W/m^2. Estimate the equilibrium warming for a doubling of CO2.

options.label: About 0.8 K
About 3.0 K
About 1.9 K
About 4.6 K

rubric: Forcing is 5.35 x 0.693 = 3.7 W/m^2; times 0.8 gives about 3.0 K.
4.6 K comes from dividing by the sensitivity parameter instead of multiplying.

items.prompt: Emissions are 10 GtC per year, 45% stays in the atmosphere, and 1 ppm of CO2 corresponds to about 2.13 GtC. What is the expected annual rise in atmospheric CO2?

options.label: About 2.1 ppm
About 9.6 ppm
About 4.7 ppm
About 21 ppm

rubric: 10 x 0.45 / 2.13 is about 2.1 ppm.
4.7 ppm ignores the airborne fraction; 9.6 multiplies by the conversion factor instead of dividing.

items.prompt: Without feedbacks, a forcing produces 1.2 K of warming. Net feedbacks have a combined feedback factor f = 0.5, with total warming = no-feedback warming / (1 - f). What is the total warming?
rubric: 1.8 K applies a simple multiplier of (1 + f), which is not the amplification formula.

items.prompt: A station's 2020 temperature is 0.9 °C above its 1951–1980 mean. The 1951–1980 global mean was about 0.3 °C above the 1850–1900 baseline. What is the anomaly relative to 1850–1900, assuming the station tracks the global mean?
rubric: Rebasing adds the offset between baselines: 0.9 + 0.3 = 1.2 °C.
0.6 °C subtracts the offset instead of adding it.

items.prompt: Applying a simple planetary energy balance, which changes would, on their own, raise Earth's equilibrium surface temperature? Select all that apply.

options.label: A fall in planetary albedo from 0.30 to 0.29
A rise in atmospheric methane concentration
A rise in global cloud and snow reflectivity
A sustained rise in stratospheric sulfate aerosols
A 1% increase in solar output

rubric: More absorbed sunlight or more greenhouse trapping raises the equilibrium temperature.
Sulfate aerosols and higher reflectivity raise albedo and cool.

items.prompt: A student models Earth as a blackbody with no atmosphere. Absorbed solar flux averaged over the globe is 238 W/m^2, and the planet must emit the same flux. Using σ = 5.67e-8 W/m^2/K^4 and flux = σT^4, what equilibrium temperature results?

options.label: About 180 K
About 375 K
About 288 K
About 255 K

rubric: 288 K is the observed surface mean, not the no-greenhouse value.

items.prompt: The seasonal swing in atmospheric CO2 is much larger at Mauna Loa (Northern Hemisphere) than at the South Pole. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?

options.label: Fossil fuel burning in the north varies strongly by season and produces most of the swing
The Southern Ocean absorbs CO2 only in winter, which cancels out the seasonal swing near the pole
The Northern Hemisphere has far more land vegetation whose growing-season uptake dominates the cycle
Sunlight at the South Pole is too weak for CO2 to be measured with the same precision

rubric: Seasonal photosynthesis and respiration on large northern land masses drives the swing.
Fossil emissions are not the main seasonal driver.

items.prompt: Which observation best distinguishes fossil-fuel combustion from ocean outgassing as the cause of the rise in atmospheric CO2?

options.label: Total CO2 in the atmosphere is increasing every year, consistent with either source equally
Seasonal CO2 swings are larger in the north, consistent with fossil use in industrial regions
Atmospheric O2 is declining in step with the CO2 rise, consistent with combustion consuming oxygen
Ocean surface pH is rising as it takes up less CO2, consistent with outgassing to the atmosphere

rubric: Burning fuel uses O2, while ocean outgassing would not lower it.
The oceans are actually acidifying, which contradicts outgassing.

items.prompt: Observations show the troposphere warming while the stratosphere cools. Why does this pattern argue against increased solar output as the main cause?

options.label: Stratospheric cooling comes only from ozone loss, which is unrelated to the question of solar versus greenhouse
More solar output would cool both layers, while greenhouse gases warm the troposphere and leave the stratosphere alone
Solar output changes only affect the stratosphere, so tropospheric warming must come from another source
More solar output would warm both layers, while added greenhouse gases trap heat below and cool the layer above

rubric: A brighter Sun would heat the whole column; greenhouse trapping shifts heat balance between layers.
Ozone loss contributes but does not remove the diagnostic pattern.

items.prompt: A student says ice cores show CO2 lagging temperature by several centuries at deglaciation, so CO2 cannot drive warming. What is the flaw in this reasoning?

options.label: The lag proves temperature causes CO2, and CO2 then has no radiative effect once it is in the air
Temperature and CO2 are measured from different cores, so no timing relationship can be drawn from them
Orbital changes began the warming and CO2 then amplified it, so a lag does not rule out CO2 forcing
Air is trapped in ice at the same time as snow falls, so the lag is an artefact that vanishes once corrected

rubric: CO2 can be both a feedback and a forcing; physics says it absorbs infrared.
The last distractor wrongly assumes causation runs only one way.

items.prompt: Surface warming flattens for a decade while ocean heat content keeps rising and Earth's energy imbalance stays positive. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: Internal variability moved more heat into the deeper ocean, so the long-term energy gain continues
Ocean heat content is rising mainly from seafloor geothermal heating, so the greenhouse effect is not the cause
The energy imbalance is an instrument error, since a true imbalance would force surface warming each year
The greenhouse effect saturated, so extra CO2 no longer traps heat and the ocean is catching up

rubric: Positive imbalance plus rising ocean heat means energy is still accumulating, just redistributed.
Saturation is a myth; geothermal flux is far too small.

items.prompt: Which observations are more consistent with enhanced greenhouse warming than with an increase in solar output? Select all that apply.

options.label: Night-time minimum temperatures rising faster than daytime maxima
Total solar irradiance rising steadily since 1980
Satellite spectra showing less outgoing longwave radiation in CO2 absorption bands
Stratospheric cooling alongside tropospheric warming
Warming limited to daytime in summer only

rubric: These are fingerprints of trapped infrared radiation.
Solar irradiance has been flat or slightly falling since 1980.

items.prompt: A coastal city's tide gauge records relative sea level rising 4.5 mm/yr, while satellite altimetry gives a global mean rise of 3.3 mm/yr. Geological surveys show the city sits on a compacting river delta. What best explains the gap?

options.label: Local land subsidence adds to the global rise in the relative sea level the gauge measures
Thermal expansion is stronger at the city's latitude, so the satellite value must be an underestimate
Tide gauges respond to atmospheric CO2 directly, so they read higher than satellite records
The satellites measure ice melt only and exclude ocean warming, so the global mean is biased low

rubric: Tide gauges measure sea level relative to land, so sinking land adds to the signal.
Altimetry measures total sea surface height, including thermal expansion.

items.prompt: In several glacial-to-interglacial transitions, ice-core records show Antarctic temperature starting to rise slightly before CO2 does. What is the best interpretation for the role of CO2?

options.label: CO2 has no radiative effect on temperature, because an effect cannot follow its supposed cause in the record
The lead is an artefact of gas-age offsets, so CO2 must in fact have driven the initial warming in every case
Orbital forcing started the warming, and CO2 released from the warming ocean then amplified it as a positive feedback
CO2 and temperature rose independently, because the carbon cycle is decoupled from the climate on orbital timescales

rubric: Orbital changes triggered the warming; the CO2 rise then amplified it, so CO2 acted as both a response and a feedback.
Distractors assume causality runs in only one direction or dismiss the lag as an error.

items.prompt: Observations show the troposphere warming while the stratosphere cools. Why does this pattern point to greenhouse gases rather than a brighter Sun as the main driver?

options.label: A brighter Sun would warm only the surface, whereas greenhouse gases heat the stratosphere directly through ozone absorption
A brighter Sun would cool the troposphere through more evaporation, whereas greenhouse gases would warm it by trapping heat
Greenhouse gases reflect sunlight back from the stratosphere, whereas extra solar output would be absorbed in the troposphere
A brighter Sun would warm the whole atmosphere, whereas greenhouse gases trap heat low down and reduce the heat reaching the upper layers

rubric: Increased solar output warms both layers; greenhouse trapping warms the lower layer while less upward radiation cools the stratosphere.
Distractors invent wrong mechanisms such as ozone heating, reflection, or evaporation cooling.

items.prompt: Water vapour is the strongest greenhouse gas, yet climate scientists treat it as a feedback and not as a primary forcing. What is the key reason?

options.label: Its concentration is fixed by ocean chemistry over centuries, so it responds only to long-term carbon cycle changes
Its lifetime is only days, so its concentration is set by temperature and cannot be raised independently
It absorbs infrared far less strongly than CO2 per molecule, so its overall effect is minor and acts only through clouds
Human activities emit no water vapour at all, so it has no route to change the climate system at any scale

rubric: Water vapour condenses and rains out within days, so its amount follows temperature, amplifying warming from other forcings.
Distractors misstate its strength, its sources, or its timescale.

items.prompt: As atmospheric CO2 rises, the fraction of each year's emissions absorbed by the ocean surface tends to fall. Which chemical explanation best accounts for this?

options.label: Rising CO2 raises ocean pH, so carbonic acid becomes less soluble and escapes back to the atmosphere
Uptake consumes carbonate ions, which lowers the buffering capacity that converts dissolved CO2 into bicarbonate
Marine plankton photosynthesis shuts down at higher CO2, so the biological pump removes less carbon to depth
Warmer water holds more gas, so the surface layer reaches physical saturation at a fixed amount of dissolved CO2

rubric: Dissolving CO2 uses up carbonate, so buffering weakens and the Revelle factor rises, reducing the fraction taken up.
Distractors confuse the effect with simple saturation, a biological collapse, or the wrong direction of pH change.

items.prompt: A commentator says the urban heat island effect explains the global surface warming trend. Which finding best shows the weakness of this claim?

options.label: City stations are nearly always adjusted upward during processing, so the raw records actually show a cooling trend that adjustments have hidden
Urban heat islands raise nighttime temperatures only, while global mean temperatures are calculated from daytime maximum readings alone
Heat islands cool the surrounding rural land through heat transfer, so their net effect on the global mean averages out to zero
Urban land is a small share of the globe, and rural-only stations, ocean temperatures and satellites show similar warming

rubric: Independent datasets that exclude cities still show warming, and urban land is a tiny fraction of the globe.
Distractors misstate how adjustments, daily means and heat island effects work.

items.prompt: Which observations help show that the rise in atmospheric CO2 comes mainly from fossil fuel burning rather than from the ocean or volcanoes? Select all that apply.

options.label: Surface ocean pH is falling, which shows that the extra CO2 originates from burning fuel
Atmospheric O2 is declining slightly, in proportion to the oxygen consumed by combustion
Atmospheric CO2 is becoming depleted in 14C, because fossil carbon has no radiocarbon left
The 13C/12C ratio of atmospheric CO2 is falling, matching the isotopic signature of plant-derived carbon
The seasonal CO2 cycle is larger in the Northern Hemisphere, which shows the added CO2 is fossil in origin

rubric: Isotope ratios and falling O2 are source-specific fingerprints of burning old organic carbon.
Falling ocean pH follows from any CO2 increase, and the seasonal cycle reflects vegetation, so neither identifies the source.

items.prompt: A student analyses an energy budget. Over a century the effective radiative forcing rose to 2.0 W/m^2, the planet warmed 1.1 K, and the current ocean heat uptake imbalance is 0.6 W/m^2. Doubled CO2 gives 3.7 W/m^2. Using F - N = lambda x dT, what is the best estimate of equilibrium sensitivity?

options.label: About 3.4 K, found by dividing 3.7 by the observed 1.1 K warming directly
About 2.0 K, found by scaling 1.1 K by 3.7/2.0 and ignoring the ocean term
About 2.9 K, from lambda = (2.0 - 0.6)/1.1, then 3.7/lambda
About 1.1 K, because the observed warming already equals equilibrium warming

rubric: Subtract the heat uptake to get the net imbalance driving warming: lambda is about 1.27, so sensitivity is about 2.9 K.
Distractors ignore the ocean heat uptake or treat the transient warming as equilibrium.

items.prompt: A blogger claims that CO2 absorption is already saturated, so adding more CO2 cannot warm the planet. Which critique is the strongest?

options.label: Saturation is real for CO2, but extra warming comes entirely from water vapour added by human activity
Absorption bands broaden as the air warms and pressure shifts, so saturation is cancelled by the warmer climate that results from extra CO2
Higher CO2 raises the altitude at which radiation escapes to space, where it is colder, so emission falls even with saturated band centres
Saturation holds in the lower atmosphere, and the thin, cold upper atmosphere has too few CO2 molecules to absorb any more infrared there

rubric: Emission to space occurs from higher, colder layers as CO2 rises, and band wings keep absorbing, so outgoing radiation falls.
Distractors misplace where saturation applies or credit the effect to another gas.

items.prompt: You must rank feedbacks by how much they explain the spread in climate sensitivity across models, given a goal of narrowing projections. Which uncertainty should research prioritise?

options.label: The water vapour feedback, since models disagree widely on how humidity changes with temperature
The Planck response, since models differ most in how blackbody emission rises with temperature
The lapse rate feedback, since it is the largest single source of the spread among models
The low-cloud feedback, since changes in cloud cover and reflectivity differ most among models

rubric: Low-cloud responses are the largest source of inter-model spread in sensitivity.
Other feedbacks are better constrained by physics and observation.

items.prompt: Criteria: lowering peak warming within 20 years, treating methane (lifetime about 12 years) fairly against CO2. Which metric is the most appropriate for comparing the two gases?

options.label: GWP500, because long horizons treat both gases equally once methane has fully decayed
GWP20, because methane's strong but short-lived forcing matters most over the near-term horizon being targeted
Mass of emissions alone, because the warming from a gas depends only on how many tonnes are released
GWP100, because it averages over a longer horizon and so represents the cumulative effect on sea level

rubric: A 20-year horizon captures methane's strong near-term warming, which matches the stated goal.
Distractors choose horizons or measures that ignore the short lifetime.

items.prompt: A team wants sea surface temperatures from 50 million years ago. Criteria: the record must reach that age, represent the ocean, and be cross-checked. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Historical ship logs and diaries, calibrated against modern thermometers to extend instruments back in time
Marine sediment proxies such as TEX86 and Mg/Ca in foraminifera, compared against each other
Deep Antarctic ice cores, since their bubbles preserve both temperature and gas for tens of millions of years
Tree-ring widths from fossil forests, since they give annual and continuous records of ocean surface conditions

rubric: Marine sediments reach that age and several independent proxies can be cross-checked.
Ice cores reach only about 800,000 years; tree rings and logs are far too young or not oceanic.

items.prompt: Criteria for a proposed solar aerosol injection plan: it should cut temperature, address ocean acidification, and avoid dangerous rebound. How should the plan be judged?

options.label: Strong, because it would offset warming and acidification together by changing how much light reaches the ocean
Incomplete, because it leaves ocean acidification untouched and risks rapid rebound warming if stopped suddenly
Strong, because any rebound after stopping would be gradual and small, so continuity risk is negligible
Weak, because aerosols cannot cool the surface at all, since they absorb as much heat as CO2 traps

rubric: Aerosols reflect sunlight but leave CO2 and acidification untouched, and sudden termination causes fast warming.
Distractors overstate the benefits or deny the cooling effect.

items.prompt: A study estimates equilibrium climate sensitivity from the 1850-2020 temperature record alone. Which are valid criticisms of this approach? Select all that apply.

options.label: Feedback strength can change as the pattern of sea surface warming evolves, so past ratios may not hold
Aerosol forcing is poorly known, so the net forcing used in the calculation is uncertain
Atmospheric CO2 before 1958 is unknowable, so no forcing can be estimated at all
Ocean heat uptake means the warming so far is transient, not yet equilibrium
The observed warming is too small to be separated from natural variability over this period

rubric: Forcing uncertainty, transient response and pattern effects each limit the sensitivity inferred from the record.
Ice cores constrain earlier CO2, and the long-term warming is clearly detectable.

items.prompt: An adviser must choose one carbon removal method for a fund. Criteria: storage that lasts over 1,000 years, quantity that can be measured and verified, and no reversal by fire or land-use change. Four options are on the table. Which best satisfies all three?

options.label: Direct air capture with deep geological injection, since storage is mineral and metered
No-till soil management on existing farmland, since soil carbon builds up steadily year after year and is checked by sampling
Biochar applied to fields, since charred biomass resists decay and is weighed before it is applied to the soil
Afforestation of degraded land, since tree growth takes up large amounts of CO2 and satellites can track canopy carbon

rubric: Geological storage is long-lived, metered at injection, and not exposed to fire or land change.
Forests and soils can be reversed and are hard to verify, and biochar durability is shorter than 1,000 years.

items.prompt: A commentator claims CO2 absorption is 'saturated' in its main infrared band, so added CO2 cannot warm the surface. Which critique best evaluates the claim?

options.label: Saturation is real, but water vapour feedback supplies all the warming, so extra CO2 itself adds no direct forcing
Laboratory tubes show absorption rising linearly with concentration, so atmospheric forcing must also rise linearly without limit
Band-wing absorption keeps growing and emission to space comes from higher, colder layers, so more CO2 cuts outgoing radiation
Saturation holds only at the surface, so the upper atmosphere absorbs the extra infrared and re-emits it downward more strongly

rubric: Adding CO2 raises the effective emission altitude and strengthens wing absorption, so outgoing radiation falls even with a saturated band centre.
Distractors confuse surface-level saturation with top-of-atmosphere balance or assume forcing is linear rather than roughly logarithmic.

items.prompt: Energy-budget estimates of equilibrium climate sensitivity from 1850-2020 data often fall below model and paleoclimate estimates. Judged on being physically grounded and testable, which explanation is best?

options.label: Ocean heat uptake is negligible, so the budget method divides by too large a heat term and biases sensitivity low
Historical CO2 forcing is overestimated because the logarithmic forcing law fails below 400 ppm, so the inferred sensitivity comes out too low
Feedback strength depends on the warming pattern, and recent patterns have had less amplifying net feedback than equilibrium will
Paleoclimate states include ice sheets, so their feedbacks can never be compared with modern feedbacks in any way

rubric: The pattern effect means feedbacks vary with the warming pattern, so the historical record can understate equilibrium sensitivity, and this can be tested in models.
Distractors rely on wrong claims about ocean heat uptake, the forcing law, or an absolute incomparability of paleoclimate.

items.prompt: Researchers want evidence that best discriminates greenhouse-gas warming from an increase in solar output as the cause of recent warming. Which observation is the strongest discriminator?

options.label: Stratospheric cooling alongside tropospheric warming, since extra solar output would warm both layers
A rising global mean temperature since 1900, since solar output has been flat or declining over most of that period
Land warming faster than ocean, since the ocean's heat capacity would respond differently to greenhouse gases than to the sun
Stronger Arctic amplification, since ice-albedo feedback would be triggered by greenhouse gases but not by solar forcing

rubric: Greenhouse gases trap heat below and cool the stratosphere, whereas more solar input would warm both layers.
Other distractors describe patterns that either forcing could produce or overstate what solar forcing cannot do.

items.prompt: A country holds methane emissions constant for 30 years. Judged by how well an accounting metric tracks the resulting temperature response, which evaluation of GWP100 is best?

options.label: It is accurate, since GWP100 weights each year's emissions by the warming they cause within that same year, matching the temperature response
It is irrelevant, because methane's radiative efficiency per molecule is lower than CO2's, so its emissions cannot matter for long-term warming
It overstates ongoing warming, because constant emissions of a roughly 12-year gas give stable concentrations and little added warming
It understates warming, because methane's short lifetime means each year's emissions build up in the atmosphere in the same way CO2 does

rubric: For a short-lived gas, constant emissions give near-constant concentration and forcing, so GWP100 treats them like a persistent CO2 stream and overstates added warming.
Distractors assume methane accumulates like CO2 or misstate how GWP100 weights emissions.

items.prompt: A blogger notes that in ice cores CO2 changes lag temperature changes by centuries at deglaciations, and concludes CO2 never drives climate. Which critique is best?

options.label: A lag shows CO2 was only a passive response to warming, so it had no radiative effect during deglaciations at all
Orbital changes usually started deglaciation and CO2 then amplified it, so a lag fits a feedback and CO2 still matters
The lag is mostly a dating artifact that better chronologies remove, so CO2 must have led temperature at every deglaciation
Ice-core air is younger than the ice around it, a correction that roughly cancels the lag and shows CO2 led temperature

rubric: Feedback loops can have a trigger then amplification, so a lag is consistent with CO2 acting as a strong amplifier.
Distractors treat the lag as proof of no effect, or invent a cancellation or artifact.

items.prompt: Which are valid reasons that global mean surface temperature alone is an incomplete measure of Earth's energy imbalance? Select all that apply.

options.label: Aerosol and cloud changes can alter the imbalance with little immediate surface signature
Most excess heat is stored in the ocean, which surface temperature barely reflects
Surface temperature cannot be measured to better than about 1 °C globally
Internal variability such as ENSO shifts surface temperature with little change in the top-of-atmosphere balance
Nearly all excess heat stays in the lower atmosphere, where surface records capture it

rubric: The ocean holds most excess heat, and variability and forcing changes decouple surface temperature from the imbalance.
Distractors misstate measurement precision or where the heat is stored.

items.prompt: Two studies fit the same observed 1.1 °C warming with a simple energy-balance model. Study A assumes aerosol forcing of -0.4 W/m2; Study B assumes -1.2 W/m2. Both use the same greenhouse-gas forcing and ocean heat uptake. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.label: Study B implies higher sensitivity, since net forcing is smaller and the same warming needs a larger response per unit forcing
Study B implies lower sensitivity, since stronger aerosol cooling shows the climate responded weakly to the forcing applied
Both imply the same sensitivity, since the observed warming fixes the climate response whatever aerosol forcing is assumed
Study A implies higher sensitivity, since weaker aerosol cooling leaves a larger net forcing and so a larger response per unit

rubric: With stronger aerosol cooling, net forcing is smaller, so matching the same warming requires higher sensitivity.
Distractors reverse the direction or ignore that sensitivity depends on net forcing.

items.prompt: Design a test using only atmospheric measurements to show that rising CO2 comes from fossil-fuel burning rather than ocean outgassing. Which design meets this?

options.label: Measure the seasonal CO2 amplitude at one station, since growth in amplitude proves the source is fossil fuel
Track δ13C of CO2 and the O2/N2 ratio together, since combustion lowers both while outgassing would not consume O2
Map the north-south CO2 gradient at many stations, since higher northern values prove fossil origin rather than ocean
Track CO2 and global temperature together, and call the source fossil if CO2 changes lead warming

rubric: Fossil carbon is 13C-depleted and combustion consumes O2, so both falling together separates burning from ocean outgassing.
Distractors use signals that show where or when, not what kind of source.

items.prompt: You need Eocene tropical sea-surface temperatures from a deep-sea core below the carbonate compensation depth, so the sediment contains no carbonate. Which proxy design fits these constraints?

options.label: Sr/Ca ratios measured in preserved coral skeletons
δ18O measured on planktonic foraminiferal shells
TEX86 from archaeal membrane lipids
Mg/Ca ratios measured in foraminiferal calcite

rubric: TEX86 uses organic lipids that survive without carbonate and records sea-surface temperature.
The other proxies need carbonate shells or coral, which this core lacks.

items.prompt: A modeller represents ocean CO2 uptake with one reservoir relaxing on a single 50-year timescale, yet observations show part of emitted CO2 persisting for millennia. What must the redesigned model add?

options.label: A land sink that saturates almost instantly, so that net uptake stops within a few years of emission
A larger single reservoir with the same 50-year timescale, so that uptake scales in proportion to emissions
An ocean-warming feedback that removes CO2 faster from the surface, so that the long tail disappears
Slower processes such as deep-ocean mixing, carbonate buffering and weathering, giving several timescales

rubric: The long tail needs multiple timescales from deep mixing, ocean chemistry and sediment and weathering processes.
Distractors keep a single timescale or invent mechanisms that cannot produce a long tail.

items.prompt: Using a climate model, you must separate effective radiative forcing from the net feedback parameter. Which experimental design meets this?

options.label: Hold sea-surface temperatures fixed and regress ocean heat uptake on CO2, so the slope gives the feedback parameter
Run an abrupt 4xCO2 run and regress net top-of-atmosphere imbalance on warming: intercept is forcing, slope is feedback
Run a long unforced control and regress imbalance on temperature, so the intercept gives the forcing
Run a 1% per year CO2 increase to doubling, then divide the final temperature by the CO2 change to get the forcing directly

rubric: Regressing imbalance on warming after abrupt CO2 quadrupling gives forcing at zero warming and feedback from the slope.
Distractors use experiments that cannot separate the two terms.

items.prompt: A proposed plan halves global CO2 emissions by 2050 and holds them there, claiming temperatures will then stabilize. What essential element is the plan missing?

options.label: A methane-only cut, since CO2 has little lasting effect once emissions are halved
A concentration target only, since temperature responds to concentration and emissions do not matter
A solar component, since halved emissions halve the radiative imbalance immediately
Net-zero CO2, since warming tracks cumulative emissions and keeps rising while net CO2 is added

rubric: Warming scales roughly with cumulative CO2, so stabilization requires net-zero CO2.
Distractors treat emissions cuts as instantly halving the imbalance or ignore accumulation.

items.prompt: Design a monitoring plan to robustly detect a long-term weakening of Atlantic overturning circulation against natural variability. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: One high-quality ship section repeated only once after five years
A continuous trans-basin mooring array measuring density-based overturning transport
A multi-decade record length so trends can be separated from internal variability
Sustained subsurface temperature and salinity profiling by floats across the basin
A single SST-based fingerprint, such as a subpolar cold anomaly, as sole evidence

rubric: Direct transport, subsurface structure and long records together detect a trend against variability.
A single SST fingerprint or a one-off section cannot establish a robust trend.

items.prompt: A planning group is told that stratospheric aerosol injection is being used to hold temperature down while emissions fall. They must design an exit plan that avoids rapid warming (termination shock) and does not rely on unproven carbon removal. Which plan meets both constraints?

options.label: Phase injection down over decades in step with deep emissions cuts, so CO2-driven warming is not released suddenly
Stop injection at once once emissions peak, since the aerosols clear and temperature settles to the new equilibrium
Keep injection constant and cut emissions only to a fixed level, because aerosol cooling offsets CO2 permanently
Double injection before stopping, since a larger buffer prevents any warming when injection ends

rubric: Aerosols last about a year, so abrupt cessation unmasks the CO2 forcing; gradual phase-down paired with emissions cuts avoids the shock.
Distractors assume aerosols are permanent or that larger doses prevent a later rebound.
